CHIEF COMPLAINT
Worsening headaches and consultation for newly diagnosed pituitary lesion with evaluation for possible surgical intervention.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS
This is a 52-year-old male presenting for neurology consultation at the request of Dr. Henry Howard for evaluation of a newly diagnosed pituitary lesion and possible surgical intervention. The patient initially presented to his primary care provider, Dr. Howard, on 3/1/21 complaining of worsening headaches over the past few months. He denied any prior history of headaches.

The patient describes the headaches as located behind the eyes with a dull nagging quality. Onset was gradual approximately three months ago with progressive worsening. Initial severity was 3/10 at onset, currently 6/10. Headaches tend to be worse in the morning and last a few hours at a time. Patient reports nothing makes them better or worse and denies radiation of pain. Recently patient has noticed bumping into door frames. He denies associated nausea, fever, rash, neck stiffness, numbness, tingling, syncope, changes in vision, or balance problems. Eyes were checked in the fall. Patient tried Tylenol a few times without improvement and discontinued.

Workup for worsening headaches was initiated with brain MRI and serology, with pituitary lesion incidentally discovered. Laboratory studies dated 3/3/21 included CBC, BUN/creatinine, coagulation, and CRP, all normal. Pituitary hormone profile demonstrated low TSH with all other results normal. MRI of brain with contrast dated 3/4/21 reveals pituitary lesion with elevation and compression of optic chiasm. Ventricles are normal in size with no other abnormalities noted.

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS
Denies nausea, fever, rash, neck stiffness, numbness, tingling, syncope, change in vision, and balance disturbance.

PAST MEDICAL HISTORY
Unremarkable. Patient denies current medical problems.

MEDICATIONS
No regular medications. Patient tried Tylenol a few times for headaches without improvement and discontinued.

ALLERGIES
Not discussed.

FAMILY HISTORY
Patient was adopted and has no knowledge of family medical history.

SOCIAL HISTORY
Works as a computer programmer. Married for 25 years. Recently purchased a small house. Denies alcohol, tobacco, and recreational drug use, stating he has never used these substances.

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION
Patient is alert and oriented to time, place, and person. Affect is appropriate and speech is fluent. Cranial nerve examination is grossly intact. No focal motor or sensory deficit in upper or lower extremities. Visual acuity is normal. Eye movements are normal. Pupils are equal and reactive. Visual field testing reveals bitemporal hemianopia. Color vision is normal.

RESULTS
Laboratory studies dated 3/3/21:
- CBC: Normal
- BUN/creatinine: Normal
- Coagulation: Normal
- CRP: Normal
- Pituitary hormone profile: Low TSH, all other results normal

MRI of brain with contrast dated 3/4/21:
- Well-defined pituitary lesion with elevation and compression of optic chiasm
- Normal ventricles
- No other abnormalities noted

Visual field testing: Bitemporal hemianopia

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN
Benign appearing pituitary adenoma incidentally discovered during workup for worsening headaches. Patient is symptomatic with clinical and radiographical evidence of optic chiasmal compression. Surgical intervention to excise and decompress the pituitary fossa is indicated via transsphenoidal approach.

Risks of anesthesia discussed including myocardial infarction, stroke, and death. Surgical risks discussed including infection, need for further surgery, cerebrospinal fluid leak or infection potentially requiring prolonged hospitalization or additional procedures, seizure, stroke, permanent numbness, weakness, difficulty speaking, and death.

Plan:
1. Patient referred to surgery scheduler (Deborah) to arrange surgical scheduling
2. Visual field testing to be arranged prior to surgery for baseline assessment
3. Referral to eye doctor for comprehensive eye examination
4. Post-operative visual field testing for comparison to assess for visual recovery
5. Pathology of resected adenoma to confirm diagnosis
6. Patient counseled regarding possibility of visual recovery post-operatively
7. Patient instructed to call with any questions
